subject: Proposal: connection lane options for Pelican Health private deploy
messages:
From: Sara Kim <sara.kim@pelicanhealth.com>
To: Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai>
Cc: John Ellis <john.ellis@pelicanhealth.com>
Date: Sat, 11 Apr 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Initial ask — connectivity lanes for private deployment

Hi Diego,

Thanks for taking this call last week. We kicked off an internal review for the Pelican Health pilot (EMR redaction + triage assistant) and we need your recommendation on how to get traffic from our VPCs to Redwood Private securely and with HIPAA controls. High-level constraints:

- Regulated data (HIPAA) — covered entity + BAA in place.
- Low latency target for sync calls: p95 < 80ms.
- Must preserve originating source IPs for audit and rate-limiting where possible.
- Outbound egress must go through our centralized proxy/NAT when leaving the VPC unless we explicitly choose otherwise.
- Ops would prefer a solution that minimizes changes to our route tables and security groups.

Options we are considering (from our side): VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site VPN (IPsec) to a Redwood gateway. Can you outline the pros/cons, any operational caveats (NAT, source IP, cross-account routing), and a recommended path with a short rollout plan?

We attached a very rough network map. If helpful, we can include packet volume and expected session counts for the pilot.

Best,
Sara

--
Sara Kim
Network Engineering Lead, Pelican Health
sara.kim@pelicanhealth.com
From: Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Kim <sara.kim@pelicanhealth.com>
Cc: Connor O'Brien <connor@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 11 Apr 2026 11:06:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Initial ask — connectivity lanes for private deployment

Sara — thanks for the concise constraints. I sketched an operational comparison and included a recommended default plus fallbacks. Attached: connectivity-diff-matrix.xlsx (tradeoff matrix) and a quick sketch of a hybrid fallback.

Summary (TL;DR):
- PrivateLink (interface endpoint) — recommended default for Pelican pilot if you can accept the extra ENIs and per-ENI costs. Pros: strongest isolation (no cross-account route table changes), keeps flow within AWS backbone, easiest to satisfy least-privilege exposure (interface endpoint placed in a controlled subnet). Cons: source IP is NAT'ed by the endpoint (unless using AWS Gateway Load Balancer pattern) — so you lose originating client IPs unless we take an additional step (see notes below).

- VPC Peering — lowest added per-hour cost and preserves source IPs natively. Pros: direct L3 connectivity, no NAT by default, minimal latency overhead. Cons: cross-account peering requires careful route table management, potential scale issues if Pelican has many VPCs (peering mesh complexity), and it exposes an L3 surface — you need strict security group/ACL discipline. Also, peering cannot traverse regions.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec) to a Redwood gateway — fastest to get started, good for POC. Pros: works with on-prem and non-AWS networks, preserves client IPs (if you avoid NAT on the gateway), can be encrypted end-to-end. Cons: variability in latency/throughput depending on tunnel endpoint, operational overhead for key rotation and monitoring, and you still have to manage NAT behavior if your egress policy routes through your centralized proxy.

Operational caveats and options to preserve source IPs:
- If you need the original client IPs for rate-limiting/audit, peering preserves them.
- With PrivateLink, AWS interface endpoints NAT to the ENI's private IP in the service VPC; technique to preserve source IPs is to use a Gateway Load Balancer + service in front of the Redwood endpoint, but that adds complexity and infra changes on Redwood's side. Alternatively, we can send an X-Forwarded-For equivalent and attest the mapping in audit logs, but that requires mutual trust and tooling.

Security/compliance notes:
- PrivateLink reduces attack surface because Pelican controls exactly which subnets can reach the endpoint. It maps well to HIPAA least-privilege and simplifies our attestation for the BAA because we can show per-endpoint access controls and flow logs.
- For Peering you will want explicit security group whitelists and flow logs enabled. We'll require a mutual runbook for incident response (who disables which routes/security groups).

Recommendation & rollout (pilot-first):
1) Pilot with PrivateLink in a dedicated Pelican subnet that you control. Quick to provision and keeps the initial blast radius small. (2 weeks to provision and harden with our infra team; cost: ENI + data processing).
2) If you need source-IP fidelity for production, plan a phased move to either: (a) VPC Peering to a dedicated Peering VPC (operationally heavier), or (b) implement a GWLB pattern that preserves client IPs; we can scope effort for both. (3–6 weeks additional work).
3) Keep an IPsec S2S tunnel as a hot fallback for cross-region failover or for on-prem connectivity.

Questions for you to decide:
- Is preserving original source IP a hard requirement for the pilot?
- Do you have strict egress routing in place that would force all outbound traffic through a centralized NAT/proxy?
- Expected baseline throughput (reqs/min and avg token load) so we can size endpoints correctly.

Connor and Kimberly — adding you for ops and compliance input. Happy to set a short workshop tomorrow to align.

Thanks,
Diego

--
Diego Fernandez
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
diego@redwood.ai
From: Sara Kim <sara.kim@pelicanhealth.com>
To: Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai>
Cc: John Ellis <john.ellis@pelicanhealth.com>
Date: Mon, 13 Apr 2026 08:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Initial ask — connectivity lanes for private deployment

On Sat, Apr 11, 2026 at 11:06 AM Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Sara — thanks for the concise constraints. I sketched an operational comparison and included a recommended default plus fallbacks. Attached: connectivity-diff-matrix.xlsx (tradeoff matrix) and a quick sketch of a hybrid fallback.
> 
> Summary (TL;DR):
> - PrivateLink (interface endpoint) — recommended default for Pelican pilot if you can accept the extra ENIs and per-ENI costs.

Thanks, Diego — this is exactly the level of detail we needed. A couple of follow-ups from our side:
1) Cost — Pelican's procurement wants a rough monthly cost delta for each pattern (ENI + data processing vs peering egress cost vs VPN appliance throughput). Can you include a ballpark in the matrix? We can share expected monthly ingress GBs: ~12TB for pilot.
2) KMS/Key custody — for HIPAA we must ensure keys are in our KMS (customer-managed). Does PrivateLink or peering change anything about encryption at rest or in-flight?
3) Timeline — if we go PrivateLink for pilot, can you commit to a two-week window for endpoint provisioning and validation? We have a compliance review on 4/28.

Also, looping in our CTO John for any exec questions.

Appreciate it — will attach traffic profile later today.

Sara
From: Connor O'Brien <connor@redwood.ai>
To: Sara Kim <sara.kim@pelicanhealth.com>, Diego Fernandez <diego@redwood.ai>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 12 Apr 2026 15:45:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Initial ask — connectivity lanes for private deployment

Sara — quick notes from ops/compliance side:
- Timeline: we can commit to a 2-week pilot provisioning for PrivateLink once Pelican provides VPC/subnet IDs and security group expectations. We will prioritize endpoint hardening and flow log collection.
- KMS: encryption at rest is unaffected by connectivity choice — keys are per-customer when you bring your KMS (we integrate with AWS KMS or external HSMs). We'll send a KMS integration checklist.
- Auditability: for PrivateLink we will enable enhanced VPC flow logs and application-level request IDs. If you require true source IPs for egress auditing, mark that as a production-ok requirement; we will then scope the peering or GWLB path.

Kimberly — can you review the BAA implications for PrivateLink vs Peering? My high-level view: PrivateLink simplifies the attestation surface and is preferred for initial compliance sign-off.

Sara — I'll schedule a 30-minute workshop tomorrow to collect the VPC details and traffic profile.

—Connor

--
Connor O'Brien
Head of Platform Ops, Redwood Inference
connor@redwood.ai
